entities.definition: Time is the SI base physical quantity of duration and temporal sequence. Its SI unit, the second, is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the caesium frequency ΔνCs — the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom — to be exactly 9,192,631,770 hertz (Hz = s-1): one second is the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to that transition. Exact per BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019) §2.3.1.

provenance.source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (2019): time among the seven SI base quantities; second defined by fixed ΔνCs = 9,192,631,770 Hz (2.3.1).
provenance.original_author: BIPM

entities.name: torque
entities.definition: Torque results from taking the cross product of force and lever arm distance. This vector quantity determines the rotational effect produced on an object around a specific axis.

examples: Pushing a door far from its hinges produces more torque than pushing near the hinges.
A wrench multiplies torque when force is applied at a larger lever arm.

formal.statement: Torque is the cross product of the position vector from the pivot to the point of force application and the force vector.

applications: Sizing engine crankshafts to handle maximum load stresses.
Designing bolt tightening procedures for structural assembly safety.
Optimizing wrench lengths for loosening rusted fasteners effectively.
limitations: Calculation assumes rigid bodies without deformation under load.
Depends critically on precise definition of rotation axis location.
Ignores frictional losses at pivot points in real mechanisms.

entities.name: velocity
entities.definition: Velocity is defined as the speed and direction of an object's motion. This vector quantity distinguishes itself from scalar speed by explicitly incorporating directional information to describe how position changes over time.

examples: A car that travels 120 km east in 2 h has average velocity 60 km/h east.
A satellite in a circular orbit has a velocity tangent to its path even though its speed is constant.

formal.statement: Velocity is the time derivative of position; average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time.
conditions: position measured in a chosen reference frame

applications: Navigating aircraft through wind currents for accurate flight paths.
Programming autonomous vehicles to maintain lane and speed limits.
Tracking migratory bird patterns relative to Earth's rotation.
limitations: Requires consistent coordinate system definitions across observers.
Instantaneous values can be noisy without high-frequency sampling.
Does not describe acceleration unless time derivative is taken.

entities.name: work
entities.definition: Work occurs when a force acts upon an object causing displacement. It is calculated as the dot product of force and displacement, representing energy transfer that happens only when motion results from applied forces.
